prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

2028 NHIS Questionnaire Redesign

For Everyone
Aug. 21, 2026

What to know

  • The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is proposing updates to the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).
  • NCHS is redesigning NHIS to modernize its data collection process.
  • The redesign is in response to rising costs, growing difficulty in reaching households, and the need for a more flexible and efficient survey.

Overview

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) has proposed a redesign of the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). Since 1957, NHIS has collected and analyzed health data to monitor the health of people across the country.

The proposed NHIS redesign includes—

  • Revisions to the adult and child questionnaires
  • Use of a sequential mixed-mode data collection design with self-response options

Changes to the questionnaires are intended to improve the measurement of contemporary health topics and reduce respondent burden through shorter and less complex instruments.

The redesign reflects the ongoing need to maintain a gold-standard national health survey while adapting to increasing data collection costs and respondent preferences by incorporating lower-cost, self-administered data collection modes.

NHIS was previously redesigned in 1997 and 2019.

Proposed content

Review the draft questionnaires and a brief description of the redesign (in the Federal Register) to learn more—

  • Adult Questionnaire
  • Child Questionnaire
  • Federal Register Notice

Public comment

NCHS invites public comment on all areas of the proposed redesign. Comments are especially welcome regarding—

  • Structure, length, and clarity of the revised questionnaire
  • Shift to a sequential mixed mode design
  • Proposed addition or removal of content
  • How these changes may affect data quality, usability, and trends over time

Commenters who suggest questionnaire additions are encouraged to identify the minimum question sets to meet identified data needs.

NCHS is also interested in comments on the practical utility of child-level data collection that is largely limited to domains for which all-person population estimates are desired (i.e., population estimates that have historically relied on data from both the adult and child-focused interviews).

Questions?

Email healthsurveys@cdc.gov with any questions about the 2028 redesign.

Comment submission

Written comments must be received on or before October 20, 2026.

You may submit comments, identified by Docket No. CDC-2026-1387 by any of the following methods:

  • Federal eRulemaking Portal:
    • Go to the Federal Register Notice
    • Click on the blue "Comment" button at the top to submit comments
  • Mail: Jeffrey M. Zirger, Information Collection Review Office, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1600 Clifton Road, N.E., MS-D74, Atlanta, Georgia 30329

NHIS-Teen

For Everyone
July 9, 2026

Key points

  • The National Health Interview Survey-Teen (NHIS-Teen) was an online survey of teenagers ages 12–17.
  • The survey gathered health information about teens from teens.
  • Data were collected from July 2021 to December 2023.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey-Teen (NHIS-Teen) was an online health survey of teenagers ages 12–17. Data were collected between July 2021 and December 2023. Health and survey experts from the academic research community and the federal government provided input to help the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) develop NHIS-Teen.

Invitations to participate in NHIS-Teen were sent to teenagers living in all 50 states and District of Columbia whose parent or guardian completed the NHIS Sample Child Interview and gave permission for their teenager to be invited.

Answers from parents and their children helped paint a picture of the health of teenagers living in the United States. Legislators, policymakers, and health organizations can use these data to better understand and serve the health needs of teenagers.

NHIS-Teen topics

NHIS-Teen covered questions on a variety of health topics, including—

  • Doctor visits
  • Sleep
  • Physical activity
  • Injuries
  • Mental health
  • Social and emotional support
  • Experiences with bullying and discrimination
Keep Reading Discovering Teen Health Insights with NHIS-Teen

Resources

Survey instrument

  • NHIS-Teen Questionnaire
  • Interactive Summary Health Statistics for Teens

Participant materials

  • Parent Postcard Brochure (English)
  • Parent Postcard Brochure (Spanish)
  • NHIS-Teen Survey Invitation

Access interactive data

The Interactive Summary Health Statistics for Teens provide estimates of selected health topics based on final data from NHIS-Teen.

NHIS-Teen reports

Methods

18-month release

  • Methodology Report for the 2021–2022 National Health Interview Survey – Teen 18-month File (09/2023)
  • Weighting Procedures and Bias Assessment for the 2021–2022 National Health Interview Survey – Teen 18-month (09/2023)

30-month release

  • Methodology Report for the 2021–2023 National Health Interview Survey – Teen 30-month (09/2024)
  • Weighting Procedures and Bias Assessment for the 2021–2023 National Health Interview Survey – Teen 30-month (09/2024)
  • The Impact on Bias Reduction from adding a Weighting Calibration Variable derived from a Recursive Partitioning Model (07/09/2026)

Publications using NHIS-Teen data

  • Citation list (updated 01/13/2026)

For Data Users

NHIS-Teen data can be accessed only through the NCHS Research Data Center (RDC). There is no public-use NHIS-Teen file available.

Find more information about applying for access to NHIS-Teen data on the RDC Application Process web page. You can find variable names in the NHIS-Teen questionnaire.

Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander NHIS

What to know

  • The National Center for Health Statistics conducted the Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander National Health Interview Survey (NHPI NHIS) in 2014.
  • The NHPI NHIS collected information about the health of Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders in all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

Overview

The 2014 Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander National Health Interview Survey (NHPI NHIS) was the first federal survey designed to exclusively measure the health of Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander people. NHPI NHIS collected data from about 3,000 households with one or more NHPI residents.

The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) modeled the NHPI NHIS on the National Health Interview Survey.

Using the 2014 National Health Interview Survey, NCHS collected information for the NHPI NHIS about:

  • Health status and health conditions
  • Disability
  • Access to and use of health services
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Vaccinations
  • Health-related behaviors, like physical activity and sleep
  • Characteristics and behaviors that increase the risk of illness, injury, or death (risk factors)

Contact us‎

Email nhis@cdc.gov or call (301) 458-4901 for more information.

Collecting data

Trained U.S. Census Bureau NHIS interviewers used the 2014 NHIS questionnaires for NHPI NHIS. As a result, statistics from the 2014 NHPI NHIS can be compared to 2014 NHIS statistics

  • NHPI NHIS Respondent Brochure
  • NHPI NHIS Poster

  • Health Care Access and Utilization Among Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander Persons in the United States, 2014 (08/2017)
  • Health Conditions and Behaviors of Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander Persons in the United States, 2014 (07/2017)
  • Selected Health Conditions Among Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander Adults: United States, 2014 (03/2017)

About NCHS

Jan. 7, 2026

Key points

  • CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) is the nation's principal health statistics agency.
  • Our data provide insights into the health of people across the United States and how their health changes over time.
  • Our statistics guide programs and policies to improve the health of the nation.

What we do

The National Center for Health Statistics is the nation's source for official health statistics. We collect, analyze, and share data and statistics to guide programs and policies that improve the health of people across the United States.

Keep Reading NCHS Mission, Vision, and Goals

NCHS collects data from many sources of health information.

  • Birth and death records
  • Medical records
  • Interviews with people and healthcare providers
  • Direct physical examinations
  • Laboratory testing

NCHS shares data, statistics, and analysis in multiple ways, including reports, dashboards, and data files. Visit our Schedule of NCHS Statistical Products and Reports to find recent and upcoming releases.

Our impact

NCHS is a unique public resource for data and evidence to help improve health. We are a key part of the nation's public health infrastructure—the people, services, and systems needed to promote and protect health in every U.S. community. We provide important data and statistics to identify health problems. Policymakers, public health professionals, and others use our data and statistics to develop and manage policies and programs to address these problems.

Our health statistics—

  • Measure the health of people across the country—the U.S. population—and smaller groups within our population
  • Monitor trends in health characteristics
  • Identify differences in health conditions and behaviors across groups
  • Document access to and use of the healthcare system
  • Support biomedical, public health, and health services research
  • Provide data to guide public policies and programs
  • Track the impact of major policy initiatives

Answering America's Health Questions

NCHS collects the data needed to answer important questions about health and health care in the United States.
Measuring the Nation's Health

Our commitment to confidentiality

Our work depends on the trust of the people who provide health information to us. NCHS takes every possible step to protect the confidentiality of personal information given to us.

Learn more about How NCHS Protects Your Privacy.

Leadership

National Center for Health Statistics
Carolyn Greene, M.D., Acting Director

Dr. Greene provides executive leadership and strategic direction for the center’s statistical programs and policies. Dr. Greene serves as the acting statistical official for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and senior advisor to the CDC director and HHS secretary.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the National Health Interview Survey comprehensively. Let me start with several searches and fetches in parallel.I have a strong foundation. Let me dig deeper into data access, methodology, users, and recent developments.Excellent progress. Let me fill in the remaining gaps: new NHIS components (Teen, NHPI), data linkage, the 2028 redesign, and long-term response rate trends.The search tool has hit its limit, but I can still fetch pages directly. Let me get the key CDC pages on new developments.I now have comprehensive information from CDC's official pages, legislative documents, methodology reports, and third-party sources. Here is the complete report.

---

# Research Report: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)

## 1. Verification of Your Dataset Description

Your description is accurate, with a few refinements worth noting for the record:

| Claim in your description | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Publisher: CDC / National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) | ✅ Correct. NCHS sponsors and conducts the survey; the **U.S. Census Bureau collects the data** under an interagency agreement (Title 13 U.S.C. § 8(b)) using trained Census field representatives. |
| "Nation's largest and oldest national health survey" | ✅ Correct — CDC describes NHIS as "the nation's largest and oldest household health survey." |
| Data since 1957 | ✅ Correct — first fielded July 1957. |
| "About 27,000 adults each year" | ✅ Accurate for the post-2019 design, which targets ~27,000 Sample Adult and ~9,000 Sample Child interviews annually in ~35,000 households. Actual counts vary (e.g., ~32,000 adults in 2019; ~21,000 in 2020 due to COVID; ~29,500 in 2023). |
| "Confidential, face-to-face interviews" | ⚠️ Mostly correct but needs nuance. The traditional mode is in-person household interviewing with telephone follow-up. Since September 2020, NHIS has used a **"telephone-first" mixed-mode protocol** (telephone attempted first, in-person visits for follow-up and when phone numbers are unknown). Confidentiality is statutorily guaranteed (see §6). |
| URL | ✅ Correct and current. |

---

## 2. Publisher and Organizational Context

- **Sponsor/conductor:** National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), one of CDC's centers and the **federal government's principal health statistics agency** — one of the 13 principal federal statistical agencies.
- **Data collector:** U.S. Census Bureau, under interagency agreement; Census field representatives conduct interviews using computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI).
- **NCHS mission:** "Collects, analyzes, and disseminates timely, relevant, and accurate health data and statistics to inform the public and guide program and policy decisions to improve our nation's health."
- **Contact:** nhis@cdc.gov; (301) 458-4901.

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

The NHIS rests on a 40+-year accumulation of public laws:

- **National Health Survey Act of 1956 (P.L. 84-652)**, signed by President Eisenhower on July 3, 1956 — the founding statute. It called for "a continuing survey and special studies" on the amount, distribution, and effects of illness and disability in the United States, plus research on survey methods and dissemination of results. The Health Interview Survey (first of the data systems implementing the Act) began fielding in July 1957.
- **Health Services Research, and Evaluation and Health Statistics Act of 1974 (P.L. 93-353)** — established NCHS in law and codified its mandate under **Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 242k)**, which directs NCHS to collect statistics on the extent and nature of illness and disability, determinants of health, environmental and social health hazards, health resources, and health services use and financing.
- **Heart Disease, Cancer, Stroke, and Kidney Disease Amendments of 1970 (P.L. 91-515)** — established the confidentiality provisions (now Section 308(d) of the PHSA, 42 U.S.C. § 242m(d)) that protect NHIS respondents.
- **CIPSEA** — the Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act (Title 3 of the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018, 44 U.S.C. 3561–3583) provides additional, exceptionless confidentiality protection.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act / OMB clearance:** Questionnaire changes go through the federal information-collection review process (e.g., the current 2028 redesign is under Federal Register Docket CDC-2026-1387, with public comment through October 20, 2026).

## 4. History

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1956 | National Health Survey Act signed (July 3). |
| 1957 | NHIS first fielded (July). Original data collection by the Bureau of the Census under contract. |
| 1960 | NCHS created administratively by merging the National Health Survey with the National Office of Vital Statistics; NHIS has been conducted by NCHS since. |
| 1957–1996 | "Classic" NHIS: family-based questionnaire, ~50,000 households and >100,000 persons per year at various points. |
| **1997** | Major questionnaire redesign (first since the survey's inception in essentially stable form): continuous measurement replaced one-week reference periods; Family Core + Sample Adult + Sample Child structure introduced. |
| 2014 | **NHPI NHIS**: first federal survey exclusively designed to measure the health of Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander people (~3,000 households), administered using 2014 NHIS instruments so estimates are directly comparable. |
| **2019** | Second major redesign: content restructured into annual core, rotating core, sponsored content, and emerging topics; collection per household reduced to one Sample Adult (18+) and one Sample Child (0–17); target ~27,000 adult / ~9,000 child interviews; explicit goal of enabling multi-year pooling for subgroup estimates. |
| 2020 | COVID-19 disruption: all-telephone interviewing from March 19, 2020; response rates fell sharply; a longitudinal component reinterviewing 2019 Sample Adults was added; extensive nonresponse-bias analyses published. |
| 2021–2023 | **NHIS-Teen**: online follow-up survey of 12–17-year-olds whose parents completed the Sample Child interview (data available only through the NCHS Research Data Center). |
| 2020s | Sample design periodically redesigned after each decennial census (current design implemented 2016), stratified by state. |
| **2026–2028** | **Proposed 2028 redesign** (announced via Federal Register, August 2026): revised adult and child questionnaires, shorter instruments, and a shift to a **sequential mixed-mode design with self-response options** — a response to rising costs and difficulty reaching households. Public comment open through October 20, 2026. |

## 5. Methodology and Design (Data-Scientist View)

- **Design:** Annual cross-sectional, multistage probability sample of the **U.S. civilian noninstitutionalized population** in all 50 states and D.C.; state-stratified; ~35,000 households per year; sample redesigned after each decennial census. Data collection is continuous (weekly) throughout the year; each quarter is independently representative.
- **Units of analysis (post-2019):** Household, Sample Adult, and Sample Child files. Sample Adult info is self-reported (proxy only if the adult is unable); Sample Child info comes from a knowledgeable parent/guardian.
- **Questionnaire structure (2019–2027):** (1) **Annual core** (health insurance, chronic conditions, functioning/disability, healthcare access and use, key behaviors like smoking, demographics); (2) **Rotating core** on a regular schedule (mental health, chronic pain, preventive services, physical activity, sleep, alcohol, industry/occupation, injuries); (3) **Sponsored content** from other agencies (e.g., cancer control — NCI; tobacco products — FDA; food security — USDA; immunizations — CDC/NCIRD; insulin use — NIDDK); (4) **Emerging topics** (e.g., 2019 prescription opioid use).
- **Response rates:** Long-term decline typical of household surveys. Recent final Sample Adult rates: 2019 ~59%; 2020 ~49%; 2021 ~51%; 2022 ~48%. 2020 Q2 telephone-only household response dipped to ~43%. NCHS publishes weighting procedures and nonresponse-bias assessments with each release.
- **Weighting:** Final person weights with nonresponse and population-control adjustments; variance estimation requires use of masked design strata and PSU variables (Taylor series / replicate weights); users must apply weights for population estimates.
- **Known analytic breakpoints:** Major trend breaks at 1997 and 2019 redesigns; 2020 mode effects. IPUMS NHIS provides harmonized, longitudinally comparable variables and user notes on these discontinuities.
- **Special 2020 design note:** roughly one-third of 2020 Sample Adult interviews were reinterviews of 2019 respondents — relevant for anyone doing longitudinal or trend work with 2020 files.

## 6. Confidentiality and Data-Use Terms (Preservationist/Librarian View)

- Data collected under a pledge of confidentiality; **statistical use only**. Willful disclosure is a **Class E felony** (up to 5 years imprisonment and/or $250,000 fine) under §308(d)/CIPSEA.
- Public-use files are de-identified: no direct identifiers; no state identifiers; masked strata and PSUs; age top-coded at 85+; some variables suppressed, coarsened, collapsed, or noise-infused; certain variables never released publicly (listed in restricted-use codebooks).
- Users agree to standard NCHS data-use terms: statistical reporting/analysis only; no re-identification attempts; no linking to identifiable data.
- **Restricted data access:** through the **NCHS Research Data Center (RDC)** (on-site, remote, or staff-assisted, fee-based) and **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)** (requires proposal + Census Special Sworn Status, ~6-month minimum lead time). Most external RDC users of NHIS seek state-level or detailed geographic identifiers. NHIS-Teen data are RDC-only (no public file).

## 7. Data Products and Access Channels

- **Annual public-use microdata files** (free download): ASCII and CSV data with SAS, SPSS, and Stata input statements; extensive documentation (survey descriptions, codebooks, questionnaires, methodology reports, imputed income files, paradata). Releases on CDC's NHIS site and the NCHS FTP server (ftp.cdc.gov). Questionnaires and datasets currently available through the 2025 cycle.
- **Early Release Program:** preliminary estimates on an expedited schedule ahead of annual file releases — notably quarterly **Health Insurance Coverage** reports (used by HHS/ASPE to monitor coverage trends and ACA effects), selected-estimates reports, biannual interactive estimates, and **Wireless Substitution** (cell-phone-only households) reports, including state-level wireless estimates.
- **Interactive tools:** NHIS Data Query Tool; Interactive Summary Health Statistics (adults, children, teens); interactive dashboards.
- **Linked data:** NCHS data linkage programs link NHIS respondents (with consent-based/statistical approval) to the **National Death Index (mortality follow-up)** — linked mortality files available for adults interviewed 1986 onward (public-use versions for 1986–2014 cohorts, restricted thereafter) — and to administrative data such as Medicare/Medicaid records via the RDC. NHIS also serves as the sampling frame for **MEPS** (Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, AHRQ).
- **Harmonized/derived collections:**
  - **IPUMS NHIS** (University of Minnesota): free, harmonized microdata covering surveys from the 1960s to the present, with consistent variable names, online tabulation, and detailed user notes on comparability, redesigns, and COVID-era changes.
  - **ICPSR** archives NHIS public-use files; CDC also maintains an archive of historical reports (the old "Health Statistics from the U.S. National Health Survey" series, Vital and Health Statistics Series 1–10+).
- **Geography in public files:** Census region only (plus a few large MSAs in some years); state and finer geography restricted to RDC.

## 8. Typical Users and Uses

- **Federal agencies:** HHS components track illness/disability trends and program performance; **Healthy People** objectives have drawn on NHIS more than any other data source (110+ objectives since 1995 through the current Healthy People 2030 cycle). ASPE uses quarterly Early Release insurance estimates to monitor coverage by age, race/ethnicity, and income.
- **Other federal sponsors:** NIH institutes, FDA (tobacco regulation), USDA (food security), SAMHSA, CDC programs (NCI-funded cancer control content, NIOSH occupational health, NCIPC opioids).
- **Policy evaluation:** NHIS was the flagship instrument for monitoring the **Affordable Care Act** (~86 new questions added in 2010; sample expanded in 2011 for state-level precision). A 2015 HHS Data Council review recommended NHIS as the best survey for estimates of *current* health insurance coverage (point-in-time design, detailed coverage verification, large sample, continuous fielding).
- **Research community:** epidemiologists, economists, sociologists, and demographers use public-use files for disparities research, health services research, and trends; RDC users conduct state-level and linked-record analyses (mortality, Medicare/Medicaid, MEPS linkage).
- **State and local users, journalists, advocacy organizations, and data activists:** rely on Early Release reports, query tools, and published NCHS reports (National Health Statistics Reports, Data Briefs such as the recent "Fatigue Among Adults, 2024").

## 9. Public Benefits

1. **Longest continuous national record of American health** — nearly 70 years of consistent measurement enabling trend analysis of illness, disability, behaviors, insurance, and access unlike any other source.
2. **Free, open public-use data** with no license fee and multi-format support, enabling independent analysis by anyone — a model of federal statistical transparency.
3. **Population representativeness with rich demographic detail** — the survey's defining strength is cross-tabulating health measures by age, race/ethnicity, income, education, nativity, sexual orientation, veteran status, disability, and more, making it the backbone of **health disparities measurement**.
4. **Policy accountability** — from tracking ACA-era insurance gains to quarterly uninsurance estimates, NHIS gives the public and Congress objective evidence on whether national health policies work.
5. **Population benchmarks** — NHIS estimates calibrate and validate other surveys and administrative data, and the survey feeds national health objectives, national accounts of disease burden, and research infrastructure (MEPS sampling, linked mortality files).

## 10. Limitations and Caveats for Users

- **Self-reported data** (no exams or lab tests — contrast with NHANES); institutionalized populations, active-duty military, and people abroad are excluded.
- **Redesign trend breaks** (1997, 2019, and a proposed 2028) require care in time-series analysis; NCHS publishes bridging and comparability guidance.
- **Declining response rates** (~48–51% recently vs. >90% in the early decades) mean weights and bias assessments must be consulted; NCHS publishes nonresponse-bias evaluations annually.
- **Mode changes** (2020 telephone-first era) affect comparability; documented mode experiments and evaluation reports accompany the 2020–2022 files.
- **No state identifiers in public files**; state-level analysis requires RDC access and often pooled years.

## 11. Key Sources Consulted

- CDC/NCHS NHIS homepage and About/Methods/Documentation pages (cdc.gov/nchs/nhis)
- NCHS "Current Legislative Authorities" and "Statutory Authorities of NCHS" publications
- NCHS Survey Description documents (2017, 2019, 2020, 2025) including Terms & Conditions and confidentiality edits
- 2019 NHIS Content Redesign materials (NCHS, FCSM, Healthy People 2030 data source page)
- CDC 2028 NHIS Questionnaire Redesign Federal Register notice page (Docket CDC-2026-1387)
- NHIS-Teen and NHPI NHIS program pages
- CDC RDC restricted-variables pages; IPUMS NHIS FAQ and user notes; MEPS/HHS Data Council working paper; Census Bureau NHIS program page

**Bottom line:** The NHIS is a statutory, continuously fielded, household-based national health survey — the oldest and largest of its kind — conducted by NCHS under authority tracing to the National Health Survey Act of 1956 and Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act, collected by the Census Bureau, and released as free public-use microdata with strong CIPSEA-backed confidentiality protections. It is the federal government's workhorse for monitoring population health, health disparities, and health insurance coverage, currently undergoing its third major redesign (proposed for 2028) as it adapts to cost and response-rate pressures — a development any preservationist or data librarian should track closely, since it will affect long-term trend comparability.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

I'll research current risks to this dataset: recent NCHS/CDC staffing and funding changes, any data removals, and policy shifts since January 2025.I have good staffing context. Now let me check for NHIS-specific changes: questionnaire content removals (e.g., sexual orientation/gender identity items), ICR status, and publication timeliness.Good progress. Now let me verify historical file availability/variable removals, NCHS leadership changes, and check the staffing tracker.Search limit reached, but I can still fetch pages directly. Let me check the federal staffing tracker and the AmStat "Nation's Data at Risk" NCHS profile for staffing/leadership details.The tracker is a JavaScript app (and being archived), so I'll rely on the AmStat report excerpts already gathered. Let me verify NCHS leadership status via CDC's site.I now have comprehensive evidence across all rubric categories. Here is the risk assessment for the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS).

---

# Dataset Risk Assessment: National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)
**Publisher:** CDC / National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) | **Assessment date:** October 2026

**Context baseline (verified this session):** NHIS is statutorily grounded (National Health Survey Act of 1956; Section 306, Public Health Service Act, 42 U.S.C. §242k), collected by the Census Bureau, with public-use microdata back to 1963. The 2025 cycle was collected and published (Early Release estimates May 28, 2026; final public-use files September 30, 2026), and an ICR extension/revision (OMB No. 0920-0214, exp. 12/31/2026) is in active renewal (91 FR 53869, comments due Oct. 19, 2026).

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- *All prior files remain public:* Documentation and data pages for the 2019–2025 cycles are live on CDC.gov, and the complete historical collection (back to 1963) is accessible via the CDC Archive and the NCHS FTP server (2024 files posted 6/30/2025; 2025 files posted 9/30/2026). *(cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/documentation; ftp.cdc.gov)*
- *Extensive third-party mirroring:* IPUMS NHIS (University of Minnesota) distributes harmonized microdata covering surveys from the 1960s to present; ICPSR archives NHIS files. Even a CDC-side removal would not eliminate public access to copies.
- *No documented removals of NHIS files or released variables:* Reviews of the early-2025 CDC/HHS web purges (KFF; Williams Institute; SHADAC; AJPH 2026) document removals of SOGI-related *content and tools* across HHS, but no retroactive removal of NHIS public-use files or the gender-identity variables collected in 2022–2024. The "Restored CDC" archive (restoredcdc.org) mirrors NHIS pages from the February–March 2025 purge period, indicating pages were temporarily affected and restored, but not the underlying data files.
- *Watch item:* Gender-identity variables in the 2022–2024 files now measure content the administration has ordered out of future collection; CMS's SGM clearinghouse documentation for NHIS now states "currently no questions are asked" for gender identity. Retroactive alteration of *released* files has not occurred, but the policy direction creates a plausible (unrealized) threat.

**Selection: No Known Issue.** Historical files remain fully accessible with no known alterations, and the dataset is unusually well-mirrored by academic archives. The SOGI-related policy environment is a monitoring concern, not a documented removal.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- *Collection and publication continue:* The 2025 NHIS was fielded and published. The 2026 cycle is in the field, and the Federal Register notice covers 2027 continuation plus a proposed 2028 redesign — strong evidence of institutional commitment to future collection.
- *ICR status:* Active (exp. 12/31/2026) with the extension/revision request published August 2026 and comments due October 19, 2026 — renewal is in process *before* expiration (satisfies the "No Known Issue" ICR criterion on its face).
- *Delay evidence (supports Moderate):* The 2025 final public-use files were released September 30, 2026, roughly 2–3 months later than the recent pattern (2024 files released June 30, 2025; SHADAC's 2025 review characterized the June 2025 release of 2024 full-year data as "on time"). The November 2025 shutdown and October 2025 RIF turmoil at NCHS are the likely contributors. SHADAC also flagged uncertainty about whether the October 2025 NCHS layoffs would affect NHIS.
- *Frequency reduction in preliminary products:* Quarterly Early Release estimates (a long-running product used to monitor health insurance coverage) were discontinued and replaced with biannual releases (SHADAC; current Early Release page shows "Interactive Biannual Estimates"). While the annual core files continue, this is a reduction in the cadence of a standing data product.

**Selection: Moderate Risk.** Nothing suggests termination — collection, publication, and ICR renewal are all proceeding, and the 2028 redesign signals long-term commitment. But the delayed 2025 file release and the downshift of Early Release products from quarterly to biannual cadence, occurring amid shutdown- and RIF-driven disruption, fit the rubric's "typical or intended publication date missed and/or publication delayed" better than "No Known Issue."

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- *Core quality maintained:* Sample sizes are stable (32,704 sample adults in 2024; >25,000 households in 2025), annual collection continues with the same design, and 2025 Early Release estimates appeared on schedule in May 2026.
- *Actual content reduction (supports High):* Per EO 14168, HHS requested and implemented removal of the gender identity question (and follow-up items) from the 2025 NHIS questionnaire; KFF's review of OMB change requests also documents removal of the "something else" response option/follow-up for sexual orientation items and a health-care discrimination question (SHADAC's independent questionnaire review confirms sexual orientation questions were retained in 2025 while gender identity items were dropped). This eliminates the survey's ability to disaggregate by gender identity going forward — a granularity reduction for an entire population subgroup.
- *Actual frequency reduction (supports High):* Quarterly Early Release estimates discontinued in favor of biannual releases.
- *Mitigating (supports Moderate):* These reductions are confined to one demographic domain and a secondary preliminary-estimate product; the breadth of core content (chronic conditions, disability, access, insurance, behaviors), sample size, and annual release cadence are intact. The pending 2028 redesign proposes *shorter* questionnaires — a further potential granularity reduction, but it is only proposed, with public comment open through October 20, 2026.
- *Institutional stress:* AmStat's "Nation's Data at Risk 2025" reports that ending of contracts at NCHS "particularly weaken[ed] the publication of reports and the release of data," and staff losses increase burden on remaining staff — emerging quality risk even for unaffected content.

**Selection: Moderate Risk (borderline toward High).** The core dataset's granularity, timeliness, and frequency are largely maintained, but two implemented changes — the EO-driven removal of gender identity measurement and the quarterly-to-biannual Early Release downshift — are genuine granularity/frequency reductions. I weight them as limited in scope relative to the survey as a whole, but a stricter reading of the rubric ("reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency") would justify High Risk. If further content cuts accompany the 2028 redesign, this category should be upgraded.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- *Explicit statutory authorization:* The NHIS traces to the National Health Survey Act of 1956 (P.L. 84-652) and operates under Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. §242k), which explicitly enumerates what NCHS must collect (illness and disability statistics, determinants of health, health services use, etc.). NCHS publishes its legislative authorities; the 1956 Act's mandate for a "continuing survey" is the survey's founding instrument.
- *No substitutes:* No other data collection provides NHIS's combination of national representativeness of the civilian noninstitutionalized household population, broad health content, and 70-year trend continuity. NHANES is exam-based with a much smaller sample and different purpose; ACS has no health content; MEPS actually *depends* on NHIS as its sampling frame.
- *Required for federal programs:* NHIS is the single most-used data source for Healthy People objectives (110+ objectives), the primary federal instrument for monitoring health insurance coverage (quarterly/biannual Early Release used by HHS/ASPE), and the base for ACA evaluation.
- *Caveat:* The FY26 President's Budget proposes moving NCHS out of CDC into an HHS "Office of Strategy" (AmStat) — an organizational change that does not alter the statutory mandate but is worth monitoring.

**Selection: No Known Issue.** Authorization is explicit, the collection mandate is clearly specified in statute, there are no alternative data collections that could substitute, and NHIS is required for multiple federal programs. This is the strongest-protected category for this dataset.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- *Staff losses:* AmStat's *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025* estimates NCHS lost ~10% of staffing by Fall 2025 (from a FY24 level of ~470 staff). October 2025: ~110 NCHS employees (~25% of the workforce, per AJPH and Data Foundation) received RIF notices during the shutdown; all NCHS RIFs were rescinded by November 18, 2025 under the terms of the reopening spending bill, with a federal judge calling the RIFs "illegal." Targeted areas included National Death Index staff, data security/legal standards, methodology, and communications staff — the support infrastructure behind data programs like NHIS (AJPH 2026).
- *Funding:* FY25 budget flat at $187.4M (≈2.4% real purchasing-power loss). FY26 President's Budget Request: $175M — a ~6.6% nominal / ~9% real cut, plus the proposed removal of NCHS from CDC. Parent-agency context: proposed FY26 CDC cut of 53%, ~600 CDC staff terminated in October 2025 on top of earlier 2025 workforce reductions.
- *Leadership:* NCHS is now led by an **Acting Director** (Carolyn Greene, M.D., per CDC's leadership page updated January 2026), following the departure of Director Brian Moyer; other senior leaders (e.g., the director of research and methodology) retired. This constitutes a leadership transition, though not a politically motivated removal.
- *Not meeting High thresholds:* The ~25% RIF was rescinded; the proposed budget cut (~7–9%) is below the 20% High-Risk threshold and not yet enacted; the center continues to function and release data.

**Selection: Moderate Risk.** NCHS sits at the floor of the 10–39% staff-loss band (~10% net loss through fall 2025), faces a proposed (not enacted) budget cut approaching 10%, has acting leadership after the director's departure, and endured a rescinded mass RIF targeting a quarter of its workforce. This is significant institutional erosion, but staffing, funding, and leadership have not crossed the High-Risk thresholds, and the NHIS program staff themselves were largely left intact (per AJPH and AP reporting, which noted NCHS was "barely touched" in earlier rounds relative to other CDC programs).

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- *Presidential Action-driven ICR change (supports High):* KFF and the Williams Institute document that HHS cited **Executive Order 14168** ("Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Gender Ideology..." / the "gender ideology" EO) in its OMB change requests for NHIS, resulting in removal of the gender identity question and related items from the survey beginning with the 2025 questionnaire. The rubric explicitly names "Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR)" and "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities" as High-Risk markers — this is a textbook match, already implemented.
- *Pending changes (supports Moderate):* The 2028 redesign (shorter questionnaires, sequential mixed-mode with self-response) is proposed, with public comment open through October 20, 2026 — a substantial pending change, though motivated by cost and response-rate pressures rather than ideology.
- *Mitigating factors:* No negative policy note on the NHIS site; the administration actively uses and cites NCHS statistics (e.g., NHANES data on ultra-processed foods, a stated administration priority); NHIS data collection and release continue apace; the survey's core topics (chronic disease, insurance, disability) align with, rather than conflict with, administration priorities.
- *Broader environment:* The AJPH 2026 commentary documents administration attempts to "erase archived data by removing years of data, selected survey variables, and survey documentations from many government websites," thwarted by lawsuits (AcademyHealth, City of San Francisco) — indicating active appetite for data suppression at HHS, even where NHIS itself has so far been spared.

**Selection: High Risk.** The EO 14168-driven modification of the NHIS information collection is an implemented, presidential-action-driven change to what the survey collects — squarely the rubric's High-Risk definition. The core program continues, but content is now demonstrably subject to alteration by executive order, and the pending 2028 redesign plus the documented broader data-erasure environment add to the risk.

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
*(All files 1963–2025 remain public; heavily mirrored by IPUMS/ICPSR; no retroactive alterations documented.)*

**Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
*(Collection and ICR renewal proceeding, but the 2025 final file release slipped ~2–3 months and quarterly Early Release estimates were discontinued.)*

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk**
*(Core sample, content, and annual cadence intact, but gender identity measurement was removed from 2025 onward and preliminary-estimate frequency was halved — borderline toward High.)*

**Statutory Context: No Known Issue**
*(Explicit statutory authority since 1956; unique, unsubstitutable collection; required for Healthy People, coverage monitoring, and MEPS.)*

**Staffing and Funding: Moderate Risk**
*(~10% staff loss at NCHS, proposed ~7–9% budget cut, acting director, and a rescinded RIF targeting ~25% of the center.)*

**Policy: High Risk**
*(EO 14168-driven removal of gender identity content from the questionnaire is an implemented presidential-action-driven ICR change.)*

**Overall takeaway:** The NHIS is one of the *least* endangered federal health datasets — statutorily rooted, unique in purpose, actively published, and widely archived. Its principal risks are not existential but incremental: politically driven content removal (already realized for gender identity), a slimmed early-release cadence, delayed file releases, and steady institutional erosion at NCHS. For preservation purposes, the highest-value actions are (1) maintaining independent archives of the 2022–2024 files containing gender identity variables (the content most likely to face retroactive pressure), and (2) monitoring the 2028 redesign and the FY26 appropriations outcome, both of which could shift Data Quality and Future Availability toward higher risk.
